results.corrected_title: Judge hears fair-use summary judgment arguments in music publishers' lyrics case against Anthropic
results.corrected_summary: On 21 October 2026, US District Judge Eumi Lee in San Jose heard cross-motions for summary judgment in the lyrics case that Concord, Universal Music Publishing Group and ABKCO brought against Anthropic. The publishers say Anthropic copied lyrics without permission and that Claude can reproduce them or generate competing lyrics. Anthropic says training Claude was fair use and that the record shows no market harm. Most of the judge's questions were about market harm, and she took the motions under submission without ruling.
key_facts: Hearing held 21 October 2026 in federal court in San Jose before Judge Eumi Lee
Plaintiffs: Concord Music Group, Universal Music Publishing Group, ABKCO
Publishers cited about 120,000 requests for 'synthetic lyrics' to Claude over six months
Anthropic's lawyer Sonal Mehta argued there was no harm to the licensing market or to lyric platforms
No ruling yet; motions taken under submission
Described as the first district-court fair-use weighing for AI training since Bartz and Kadrey
results.issues: Lawyer Monthly does not give the hearing date. The 21 October date comes from CMU ('yesterday' in a 22 October article), a Chamber of Progress live post and search summaries. The 'first since Bartz and Kadrey' claim comes from the ChatGPT Is Eating the World tracker. The 'first case to go to trial' framing in why_it_matters is speculative.

results.corrected_title: Reservoir Media sues Anthropic and Suno as AI copyright filings hit a weekly record
results.corrected_summary: On 21 October 2026, Reservoir Media filed separate copyright and DMCA suits against Anthropic and Suno in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Against Anthropic it alleges that lyrics to 853 of its compositions were used to train Claude, and against Suno it alleges 1,050 works were copied. The ChatGPT Is Eating the World tracker counted eight new AI copyright suits that week, a record, bringing the total to 156. Separately, Canadian publishers' suit against Anthropic in Ontario was widely reported on 19 October, but it was filed on 6 October.
key_facts: Reservoir v. Anthropic and Reservoir v. Suno filed 21 October 2026 in N.D. California, by the law firm Adams & Reese
Anthropic suit covers 853 works; reported damages sought are about $151 million (about $128M for infringement plus $23.5M under the DMCA)
Suno suit covers 1,050 works; about $186 million sought
Tracker: 8 new AI copyright suits in one week, a record; 156 in total
Canadian suit (Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, The Canadian Press) was filed in Ontario on 6 October 2026 and reported by The Canadian Press on 19 October
results.issues: The Canadian publishers' suit is stale: it was filed on 6 October 2026, before the window, and first reported by Cartt.ca on an unconfirmed date. The CP/CTV story is from 19 October, but the CTV page body would not load and CBC returned 403, so the filing date and plaintiffs come only from search summaries. The '21 October' filing date for the Canadian suit in the original item is wrong. I reframed the item around the in-window Reservoir suits and the record week. The tracker names only 3 of the 8 cases, so the 'record' is the tracker's own claim. The total damages figures come from search summaries and differ slightly between outlets.

results.corrected_title: UK FCA official: firms should report significant AI failures and near-misses
results.corrected_summary: Jessica Rusu, the FCA's Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer, said in a speech at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series on 19 October 2026 that incident-reporting rules 'must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses'. Quoting the UK AI minister, she said near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. She also said the FCA will work with industry, other regulators and frontier labs on 'a trusted framework for agentic finance' covering agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution. The speech set a policy direction and did not change any FCA rules.
key_facts: Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer
Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series, Monday 19 October 2026
Quote: incident reporting 'must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses'
Near-miss reporting for agentic AI called a 'national security priority' (quoting the AI minister)
Planned framework for 'agentic finance', developed with industry, other regulators and frontier labs; no timetable given
No new binding rules yet; the FCA did not define 'significant' before publication
results.issues: Rusu's full title is Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer, not only 'chief data officer'. The 'national security priority' wording is her quote of the AI minister, not her own claim. The 19 October date is inferred from 'Monday' in 20 October articles; I did not open the FCA speech page itself. This is a policy direction, not a rule change.
